EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure set up across western Colorado overnight from January 3 to 4, leading to clear skies and light winds. Pools of strong moisture remained within many valleys though from precipitation earlier in January. With this, cooling overnight temperatures led to a saturated near-surface environment and widespread dense fog.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread dense fog developed within valleys along I-70 during the morning of January 4. The KRIL ASOS at the Rifle Garfield County Airport reported 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog for about a half an hour between 5:30-6:00 AM. After a brief period of improved visibilities, dense fog redeveloped around 7:00 AM. Visibilities reached 1/4 mile or less for about 3.5 hours before dissipating. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad trough moved through the CONUS in mid-January with weak flow situated over Colorado. Embedded shortwaves moved through the trough, bringing bouts of active weather, including overnight from January 8 to 9. Strong snow bands developed ahead of the cold front moving through southwestern Colorado. As skies cleared and temperatures dropped behind the front, dense fog developed within some valleys near the San Juan mountains where heavy snow had occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread fog, including areas of dense fog, developed within the Animas River Basin during the morning of January 9 following heavy snowfall. The KDRO ASOS at the Durango La-Plata County Airport reported two prolonged periods of visibility being reduced to or below 1 mile. During the first period, sporadic and brief periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog occurred. During the second period which began shortly before sunrise, dense fog reduced visibility to or less than 1/4 mile for about three and a half hours before slowly dissipating through mid-morning. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The winter of 2025-2026 has been, overall, a dry and warm one. And as such, drought has clung on across eastern Utah and western Colorado, especially across the Central Divide Mountains. Areas in the eastern Uinta mountains have also seen drought linger.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front swept southward across eastern Colorado during the evening of January 15th, with it bringing wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph. Even weaker winds were reported in the foothills of Boulder County. A small corridor near the Wyoming border experienced strong winds with the strongest report being 78 mph near Virginia Dale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The winter of 2025-2026 has see precious little in the amount of snow accumulating in the mountains. When a decent storm does develop, bringing fresh snow to the higher elevations, back country skiers flock to the terrain. However, with the infrequency of accumulating snow this winter, the snowpack is overall unstable, and liable to avalanche when this new fresh snow loads on top of the older, unstable layers. At that point, all it takes is a person in the wrong place at the wrong time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: To summarize the write up provided by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center (CAIC) regarding this incident: The area of the incident is known locally as King Arthur's/Timber Falls (39.628, -106.308). 1 backcountry tourer caught and partially buried, injured. Skier triggered avalanched rated as R2 and D2, meaning it was small relative to it's path but was large enough to catch, injure or kill a person. Avalanche was below treelline and on an east facing slope. CAIC had rated the avalanche danger in that area on that day a 2/5 or moderate, mainly at or above treeline, with danger ranged 1/5 or low below treeline. North through east facing slopes rated most dangerous. 2 skiers triggered the avalanche, with only one being caught and pinned against a tree, suffering cuts and abrasions. With assistance from the other skier, who was able to avoid the avalanche, the trapped skier was freed and both were able to leave the site of the avalanche.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the days leading up to this event, a strong trough made landfall along the West Coast of the US. Ahead of this system, unusually warm and dry conditions prevailed as high pressure dominated the Intermountain West. The trough began to track inland on the 15th into the 16th, but the high pressure was reluctant to shift east. This led to a tightening up of the pressure gradient between these two features, enhancing an already strong southwesterly upper level jet. Lift began to increase ahead of the trough on the evening of the 16th, with mountain rain and snow showers breaking out over the higher terrain of eastern Utah and western Colorado. This also helped to keep deep mixing ongoing well after sunset, resulting in some of the peak winds occurring between midnight and daybreak on the 17th. In addition, a potent cold front was associated with this system, and was expected to sweep through eastern Utah and western Colorado around daybreak. Ahead of the cold front, the surface pressure gradient tightened substantially and surface winds maxed out. This coincided with the period between midnight and daybreak on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At 10:41 PM MST on February 16th, the Colorado Department of Transportation sensor 139s034 Douglas Pass recorded a gust to 86 mph. Additional gusts recorded at this sensor during the event include a second gust to 86 mph at 1:55 AM MST 2/17, and a gust to 74 at 5:29 AM MST on the 17th. Additional sensors in the zone, all RAWS, recorded gusts from 45 mph to 67 mph during the period of high winds. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received in association with these high winds.

CZ_NAME: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures and below normal precipitation continued through the month of February. This led to a continued state of drought across eastern Utah and western Colorado, particularly along the northern and central Colorado Divide mountains. Extreme (D3) Drought saw expansion during the middle of the month, moving into portions of lower elevation northwest Colorado.

Exceptional (D3) Drought covered 45% of the zone, with Severe (D2) covering 19%, and Moderate (D1) covering 1%. With the 2/11 US Drought Monitor update, Exceptional (D4) Drought remained unchanged, at 35% coverage. Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to 50% coverage, with Severe (D2) Drought shrinking to 15% coverage, and Moderate (D1) Drought being removed. From this point through the end of the month, drought conditions remained unchanged in the zone. No reports of damages or impacts from drought conditions have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A solid mid-month snow storm brought a few feet of fresh snow to the Colorado Divide mountains. This fresh snow fell atop a shallow layer of faceted, old, and unstable snow, creating an overall unstable snowpack. However, as this winter has been very snow poor, the fresh snow enticed a number of backcountry tourers, despite dangerous avalanche conditions as analyzed by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center. As a result, two avalanches resulted in injuries to two different backcountry tourers.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the accident day, the avalanche danger in the area was rated 3/5 - Considerable at all levels, below, near, and above treeline. Avalanche danger was rated on all aspects, with large to very large avalanches likely west through north to east aspects, and small avalanches possible on southwest through southeast aspects. Avalanche discussion indicated that recent avalanches in the area had been large enough to bury, injure, or kill a person, and could be triggered remotely, from a distance or below, and could travel long distances. The accident group consisted of three backcountry tourers, 1 split board rider and 2 skiers, and the intention was to ski a southwest slope from a sub-peak south of Bonita Peak into Minnehaha Basin (37.893, -107.625). Before ascending toward their destination, they stomped on several areas of drifted snow with no reaction. South slopes noted to have shallow snowpack. Rider 1 descended first and made two ski cuts with no reactivity, then started down the slope. A number of turns into Rider 1's descent the avalanche broke and the Rider was caught, tumbling end over end down the rocky path. Rider 1 came to a stop in a standing position at the bottom of the path, buried from the waist down. A second avalanche, triggered by Skier 1 in the hangfire, struck Rider 1 and pushed them further downhill, leaving them in a seated position. Skier 1, who triggered this avalanche, was also caught and carried, bouncing over rocks and left with their legs buried and an injured arm. Rider 1 was able to self-extricate and moved to Skier 1 to extricate them. Skier 2 chose to descend the way they had ascended, and all met and returned to the trailhead. The larger of the two avalanches was rated R2/D2, meaning it was small relative to its path but was large enough to catch, bury, injure, or kill a person. The smaller avalanche was rated R1/D1, meaning it was very small relative to its path and was small enough to be mostly harmless.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Relatively clear early-day skies on February 12 led to isolated convection with rain and snow showers across portions of western Colorado. Some valleys were already saturated or near-saturated due to periods of precipitation over the prior days. As such, in spite of dense cloud cover lingering overnight and lacking radiational cooling, saturated surface conditions paired with weakening winds were capable of producing areas of dense fog on the morning on February 13.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread dense fog developed within the Yampa River Basin during the morning of February 13. The KCAG ASOS at the Craig-Moffat County Airport reported two prolonged periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog and freezing fog, once before sunrise and once after. Several hours of reduced visibility above 1/4 mile due to mist and fog were also observed during the morning. The KEEO ASOS at the Meeker Coulter Field Airport observed almost three hours of 1/4-mile visibility due to freezing fog prior to sunrise. The KHDN AWOS at the Yampa Valley Regional Airport also reported several prolonged periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog and freezing fog both before and after sunrise. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure trough digging southward down the west coast along with a 180 kt jet stream allowed a significant surge of Atmospheric River moisture along with strong southwest winds to advect into eastern Utah and western Colorado. This allowed for significant mountain snowfall across most mountains in eastern Utah and western Colorado where one to two feet of snow fell. Snowfall transitioned from a heavy wet snow with lower snow ratios in the early stages to an efficient power like snow with higher snowfall ratios due to the drastically changing temperatures. Some favored southwest slopes received up to three or more feet of snow as well. The strong jet allowed for strong winds and blowing snow in addition to the heavy snow falling with gusts in the 45 to 60 mph range on average across the mountains with some localized higher gusts above 70 mph. Due to the warm airmass, most lower valleys received rain or a mix limiting accumulations except the southwest Colorado valleys that saw a combination of heavy snow and blowing snow due to the wind once they received the colder air with a second shortwave and strong cold front towards the latter half of this three day storm event.  There were also some snow squalls in some areas due to the combination of heavy snow, wind and low visibility at times with the passage of the strong cold front toward the latter half of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 11 to 20 inches of snow fell across the area with 11.5 inches reported at Steamboat Springs 2.0 ESE. Winds gusted in the 55 to 75 mph range at Storm Peak Lab with a peak wind gust of 78 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following multiple days of rain and snow showers, drier northwesterly flow on the backside of a shortwave trough brought clearer skies on the evening of February 13 into the morning of February 14. With ample surface moisture still in place from the prior days' precipitation and strong radiational cooling from clear skies, dense fog developed across many valleys.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Areas of dense fog developed within the San Juan River Basin during the morning of February 14. The KPSO AWOS at the Stevens-Pagosa Springs Airfield reported about two hours of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog following several hours of light to moderate snowfall. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure trough digging southward down the west coast along with a 180 kt jet stream allowed a significant surge of Atmospheric River moisture along with strong southwest winds to advect into eastern Utah and western Colorado. This allowed for significant mountain snowfall across most mountains in eastern Utah and western Colorado where one to two feet of snow fell. Snowfall transitioned from a heavy wet snow with lower snow ratios in the early stages to an efficient power like snow with higher snowfall ratios due to the drastically changing temperatures. Some favored southwest slopes received up to three or more feet of snow as well. The strong jet allowed for strong winds and blowing snow in addition to the heavy snow falling with gusts in the 45 to 60 mph range on average across the mountains with some localized higher gusts above 70 mph. Due to the warm airmass, most lower valleys received rain or a mix limiting accumulations except the southwest Colorado valleys that saw a combination of heavy snow and blowing snow due to the wind once they received the colder air with a second shortwave and strong cold front towards the latter half of this three day storm event.  There were also some snow squalls in some areas due to the combination of heavy snow, wind and low visibility at times with the passage of the strong cold front toward the latter half of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Douglas Pass reported 17 inches of snow. Winds gusted in the 45 to 75 mph range with a peak wind gust of 86 mph at Douglas Pass.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The County Road 169 Fire was reported at approximately 12:15 on February 17th, 2026 near Matheson in Elbert County during a red flag weather day. Crews arrived to a wind driven fast moving grass fire in dry conditions near the area of County Rd. 169 and Hwy. 24. The call was upgraded and mutual-aid was requested with evacuations due to the fire moving quickly. A combination of dry cultivated fields and short grass prairie fields provided ample fuel. The added low humidity of only 6% and high winds created a dangerous situation for all personnel. Winds were recorded at more than 70 mph, causing smoke and blowing dust to create visibility hazards. Graders were brought in and a few locals used their own equipment to assist with the firefighting efforts. After more than 5 hours, crews finally contained the fire with an approximate total of 5,598 acres burned.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure trough digging southward down the west coast along with a 180 kt jet stream allowed a significant surge of Atmospheric River moisture along with strong southwest winds to advect into eastern Utah and western Colorado. This allowed for significant mountain snowfall across most mountains in eastern Utah and western Colorado where one to two feet of snow fell. Snowfall transitioned from a heavy wet snow with lower snow ratios in the early stages to an efficient power like snow with higher snowfall ratios due to the drastically changing temperatures. Some favored southwest slopes received up to three or more feet of snow as well. The strong jet allowed for strong winds and blowing snow in addition to the heavy snow falling with gusts in the 45 to 60 mph range on average across the mountains with some localized higher gusts above 70 mph. Due to the warm airmass, most lower valleys received rain or a mix limiting accumulations except the southwest Colorado valleys that saw a combination of heavy snow and blowing snow due to the wind once they received the colder air with a second shortwave and strong cold front towards the latter half of this three day storm event.  There were also some snow squalls in some areas due to the combination of heavy snow, wind and low visibility at times with the passage of the strong cold front toward the latter half of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 12 to 36 inches of snow fell across the area with locally higher amounts up to 46 inches at Sharkstooth. 21.5 inches of snow was reported at Dolores 16.8 ENE. Winds gusted in the 45 to 55 mph range with a peak wind gust of 58 mph at Stevens Field Airport located 3 miles northwest of Pagosa Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A solid mid-month snow storm brought a few feet of fresh snow to the Colorado Divide mountains. This fresh snow fell atop a shallow layer of faceted, old, and unstable snow, creating an overall unstable snowpack. However, as this winter has been very snow poor, the fresh snow enticed a number of backcountry tourers, despite dangerous avalanche conditions as analyzed by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center. As a result, two avalanches resulted in injuries to two different backcountry tourers.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the accident day, the avalanche danger in the area in question was rated 3/5 - Considerable for areas near and above treeline. Below treeline, avlanche danger was rated 2/5 or moderate. A Special Avalache Advisory was in effect due to recent snow and strong winds forming thick, cohesive slabs over an unusually weak and shallow snowpack. Slopes with wind drifted snow were indicated as most dangerous, with deep (2-3 feet) buried weak layers giving little warning before breaking into an avlanche. Avalanches of small to large size were likely at all levels on aspects northwest through north to east, and likely near or above treeline on aspects south through southeast. The accident group consisted of 4 skiers, who had spent most of the day successfully skiing east facing slopes. For the last run of the day, the group chose a northeast-facing slope south of the Hahns Peak Lake Dam (40.830, -106.986). Skier 1 did ski cuts that were unreactive, and successfully skied the skier's left side of the slope. Skier 2 began their run and after two turns the avalanche broke. Skier two was knocked off their feet and caught, eventually tumbling before being slammed against a tree. They were headfirst on their back, with snow up to their chin, but were able to clear their mouth and wave for help. One of the remaining members of the group were able to extricate Skier 2 and help them down, under their own power but with assistance. Unknown extent of injuries. Avalanche had a 2 foot fracture line, was 30 feet wide and ran 100 feet. Avalanche occurred below treeline on a northeast-facing slope, and was rated R2/D2, meaning it was small relative to its path but large enough to catch, carry, bury, injure, or kill a person.
